pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ˈjoʊɡə/** ​— Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Yoga).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ‌**Yo-** ​— ‌From ​√yuj, “to ‌yoke, ​join”; ​the ​o ​is long ​— ‌the ​yoking ‌of the ​self ‌to ​the ‌divine.
- ​**-ga** — ‌The ​abstract ​noun: ‌the yoking ‌itself ‌— ​the ​discipline by ‌which ​union ​is ‌achieved.

​For the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: ​“YOH-guh”

​Kindred ​and ‌historical forms ‌of ​the ‌name:

- ​**Latin** — ​iugum, ‌English ‌“yoke” ‌— the ‌same ​Indo-European ‌root

​The ​word and ​English ‌“yoke” ​are ​cousins: yoga ​is ‌the ​yoke ​worn ​willingly. The ‌root ​√yuj ‌also ​yields English ‌"yoke" ​— ‌the ‌cognate pair ​has ​named ​the ​same ‌joining for ‌five ​millennia.

domains.body:
**Yoga** ​is the ‌discipline of ‌union: ​the yoking ​— ​the same ​root as ​English ‌‘yoke’ — ​of mind, ​breath, ‌and self ​to the ‌still ​point beneath ‌them. ​Born in ​the ascetic ​experiments ​of the ​late Vedic ‌age, ​codified by ‌Patañjali’s sūtras, ​it ‌is both ​one ‌of the ​six orthodox ‌schools ​of Indian ​philosophy and, ‌in ‌the Bhagavadgītā’s ‌teaching, the ​art ​of every ‌act ​done without ​attachment to ‌its ​fruit.[^1]

### The ​Eight Limbs

‌Patañjali’s ​aṣṭāṅga: restraint, ‌observance, posture, ​breath, ​withdrawal, focus, ​meditation, ​absorption.

### Union ‌of Rivers

‌The ​yogin joins ‌mind to ​breath ​to object ‌as rivers ‌join ‌the sea ‌— ​the Upaniṣadic ‌image.

### Yoga ​in ​the Gītā

​Skill in ‌action: ​the yogin ​works without ​craving ‌the fruit ​— ​karma-yoga as ​the path ‌for ​the householder.

### ‌The Cessation ​of ‌the Waves

​Patañjali’s definition: ‌yogaś ‌citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ — ​the ​stilling of ​thought’s waves, ​so ‌the seer ‌abides in ​itself.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Yoga concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Eight ​Limbs** — ​Patañjali’s ‌aṣṭāṅga: ​restraint, ‌observance, ​posture, ‌breath, ​withdrawal, ‌focus, meditation, ​absorption.
- ‌**Union ​of ​Rivers** ‌— ‌The ‌yogin ​joins mind ​to ‌breath ​to ​object ‌as ​rivers ​join ‌the sea ​— ‌the ​Upaniṣadic ​image.
- ​**Yoga ​in ‌the ‌Gītā** — ​Skill ‌in ​action: ​the ‌yogin ‌works ‌without ‌craving the ​fruit ‌— ​karma-yoga ​as ​the ‌path ​for ​the householder.
- ​**The ‌Cessation ​of ​the ​Waves** ‌— ​Patañjali’s ‌definition: yogaś ​citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ ‌— ​the ‌stilling ‌of ​thought’s ​waves, ​so the ​seer ‌abides ‌in ​itself.

mythology.body:
Yoga has ​no myths — ‌it has sūtras, ‌and the sūtras ​are their own ​literature of precision. ​Its ‘stories’ are ​the doctrine’s own ​history: the ascetics ‌in the forests ​of the Upaniṣads, ​the Nātha-lineage’s wonder-working adepts, ‌and the modern ​export that made ‌a metaphysical discipline ​into the world’s ‌most practised physical ​art.[^1]

### The Chariot ​Simile (Kaṭha Upaniṣad)

​The body the ​chariot, the senses ​the horses, the ‌mind the reins, ​the intellect the ‌driver, the rider ​the self: the ‌Kaṭha Upaniṣad’s simile ​is the oldest ‌complete map of ​the psychophysical discipline. ‌Who holds the ​reins attains the ​end of the ‌road — ‘the still ‌place from which ‌the wise do ​not return’.[^2]

### The ​Yoga of Three ‌Paths (Bhagavadgītā)

The ​Gītā democratizes the ​discipline: jñāna-yoga of ‌knowledge for the ​philosopher, karma-yoga of ​selfless work for ‌the householder, bhakti-yoga ​of devotion for ‌the lover of ​god. ‘Yogasthaḥ kuru ​karmāṇi’ — established ​in yoga, act ​— is the ‌verse on which ‌Gandhi claimed to ​have fed his ‌whole life.

### The ​One Hundred Ninety-Five Sūtras ​(Patañjali)

Patañjali’s Yoga-sūtra ‌— c. 195 ‌aphorisms — systematized ‌what had been ‌experiment: the eight ​limbs, the afflictions, ‌the meditative absorptions, ​the supernormal powers ​that are signs ​on the path ‌and traps at ​its end. Commentators ​from Vyāsa to ​the present have ‌kept it the ​living constitution of ​the discipline.

### The ​Immortal Teachers (Nātha ‌Lineage)

The medieval ​Nātha order gave ‌yoga its adepts-legend: ​Matsyendra caught among the ‌fishes, Gorakṣa the ​miracle-working founder, and ‌later figures claimed ‌to walk the ​centuries — the ​siddhas, perfected ones, ​whose bodies outlast ​death. Hatha-yoga’s physical ‌canon comes from ‌this line of ​embodied experimenters.

overview.body:
**Yoga** (*yoga*) ​— Union, ‌the Yoking ‌of Self ​to Divine · ​Union, yoking ​— spiritual ​and ascetic discipline ​by which ‌the individual ​self is ​joined to the ‌divine — ​belongs to ‌the Sanskrit ​tradition, where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Union, Discipline". ​The name ​means "Union, ​yoking — ‌spiritual and ascetic ​discipline by ‌which the ​individual self ‌is joined to ​the divine; ‌also the ​name of one ‌of the ​six orthodox ​schools of ‌Hindu philosophy."[^1].

**Yoga** ‌is the ‌discipline of ​union: the ​yoking — the ‌same root ​as English ​‘yoke’ — of ‌mind, breath, ​and self ​to the ‌still point beneath ​them. Born ‌in the ​ascetic experiments ​of the late ​Vedic age, ​codified by ‌Patañjali’s sūtras, it ‌is both ​one of ‌the six ​orthodox schools of ​Indian philosophy ‌and, in ‌the Bhagavadgītā’s ‌teaching, the art ‌of every ​act done ‌without attachment to ​its fruit.[^2]

The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description computed ‌from the ​displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII form ‌*yoga* contains ​the same ‌letters: no ‌recovered diacritics or ​special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**योग**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Union, yoking ‌— ​spiritual and ​ascetic ‌discipline ​by which ‌the ​individual self ‌is ​joined to ​the ​divine; ​also the ​name ‌of one ​of ‌the six ​orthodox ‌schools ​of Hindu ‌philosophy."[^1].

​The canonical ‌spelling ​**Yoga** matches ​the ‌conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*yoga* contains ​the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ​lost diacritics ‌or ​encoding transition ‌is ​claimed. The ​editorial ​work ​is to ‌fix ‌one reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, preserve ​capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ‌keep ‌the original ‌evidence ​visible. The ‌displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ‌**y** ​→ **Y** ‌— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **o** ​→ ‌**o** — ‌Same
- ​**g** → ​**g** ​— ​Same
